content_html:
Open source · runs in your repository

Say what the software should do. Your agent won’t forget why.

Kibi is a requirements framework for AI coding agents. It records the reasoning behind your code (the intent, assumptions and trade-offs you agreed in the chat) as requirements in your repository, links them to the code and tests, and makes every later agent respect them.

  • Keeps the why behind each change, not just the what
  • Shows the agent that reasoning before it edits the code
  • Refuses new rules that contradict old ones
  • Reports which requirements are actually tested

Each line is a requirement riding to the gate. Only fresh end-to-end evidence clears it.

01The problem

Code shows what the software does. Not what it must keep doing.

In source, every line looks equally deliberate. A hard-won trade-off, a business rule, a temporary assumption, a shortcut and a forgotten leftover all read the same. The difference lived in the conversation where they were decided, and that conversation is gone. So the next agent either “cleans up” a decision or carefully preserves an accident.

  • 01

    The why outlives the chat

    Without

    The chat said “we’ll do X to retain users”. The code only says X, and the next agent cannot tell a trade-off from a mistake.

    With Kibi

    Each requirement records why it exists, in the words of whoever asked, and decisions keep their trade-offs. When you state a rule, the agent records it in one kb_record call with your reason, your words and the code that implements it, and learns at once whether a commit would pass. They live in .kb/ beside the code on every branch, and Kibi flags requirements that do not say why.

  • 02

    Decisions stop getting undone

    Without

    The agent rewrites a rule it never knew existed.

    With Kibi

    Before it edits a file, the agent is shown the requirement that code implements, what it must keep true, why it exists, and the decision behind it.

    Conflicts are caught before the code

    Without

    Two prompts a week apart contradict each other, and nobody notices.

    With Kibi

    A rule that contradicts an existing one is refused with both named, and you decide which wins.

    “Done” means tested, not claimed

02Why not a memory file

Memory remembers. Kibi enforces.

Notes files and memory servers help an agent recall things. Kibi turns intent and its reasons into rules that are linked to code, checked for contradictions, put in front of the agent at edit time, and backed by evidence.

03How it works

From prompt to proof, on one rail

Kibi keeps intent attached to the work at every stage, and it is conservative about the last one.

  1. Intent

    You say it once

    Prompt the behavior in plain words, the way you already do. That sentence stays the source.

  2. Requirements

    The agent writes it down

    Requirements, scenarios and typed facts land in .kb/ beside the code, citing the ticket or page they came from.

  3. Enforcement

    Every edit hears it

    Hooks name the requirement before an agent edits the code that implements it. Checks flag contradictions and untraced code.

  4. Evidence

    Tests leave receipts

    A test that claims a requirement records evidence tied to the exact code snapshot it ran on.

  5. Proof

    Only fresh evidence passes

    Stale receipts and passing unit tests do not clear the gate. Proved is reserved for claims a checker established for every case.

04Your part

What you actually do

Three things, and none of them is filling in a requirements form.

  1. 01

    State the behavior

    Prompt the way you already do. “Draft edits must save when someone navigates away.” You do not fill in a requirements form.

  2. 02

    Approve real decisions

    The agent proposes a plan before it writes project knowledge. You approve it, or you correct the product call. A plan compiled from your prompt lands in full or not at all, and the bookkeeping stays with the agent.

  3. 03

    Read the result

    The health report names what is tested, what still has a gap, and what contradicts itself, and labels each requirement proved, tested, asserted or unverified. A green test run is a different fact. When the pre-commit hook refuses new code no requirement owns, it prints one block per declaration with the requirements that already own the rest of its file and a ready-to-run input that links it, never a pick of its own.

05Setup

Add Kibi to the repository

Kibi is driven by your coding agent, so the recommended setup is a prompt. Your agent installs the packages, runs kibi init, connects itself to Kibi, and bootstraps the knowledge base behind a plan you approve, then adds scenarios, predicates and the claims the plan could not write in the normal workflow, and proposes how proof runs for your test runner in a second plan you approve. The package-manager tabs are the manual route; re-running kibi init completes missing directories and schema files while preserving existing knowledge and schema files. It does not invent what the product does.

The agent first asks where your product intent lives, such as issue trackers, wikis and specs, and which sources to trust. Every requirement in the bootstrap plan cites the ticket or page it came from, and nothing is written until you approve the plan. When a claim sits next to an existing requirement on the same topic that Kibi cannot check logically, the plan names that requirement so the agent compares the two, including for claims the plan leaves for the agent to write. How plans are built, applied and resumed after an interruption is in the MCP reference.

The bootstrap records the code that decides each behavior, not every declaration. The pre-commit hook judges a commit only on the declarations it adds or changes, so an agent's correct change is never refused over gaps it did not create; kibi check counts the unrecorded rest as non-blocking symbol debt (kibi check --symbol-debt lists it), and it shrinks as commits touch that code.

Requires Node.js 22+. SWI-Prolog is bundled on Linux (x64, arm64) and macOS; other platforms need swipl (SWI-Prolog 9.0+) on your PATH. A system swipl is only a fallback; set KIBI_SWIPL=system to prefer it. Bun commands and per-platform setup are in the installation guide. Each release has one version, such as Kibi 2026.11.0, that names its exact package set; kibi --version and kibi doctor show it (release versions), and the CLI tells you once a day when a newer one is out (update notices). Kibi sends anonymous usage statistics; see what is sent and how to turn it off.

07FAQ

Questions people ask first

The short answers. The guide has the long ones.

Do I write the requirements myself?

No. You describe the behavior. Your agent turns that into requirements, scenarios, tests, and links to the code. You step in when the product decision is actually ambiguous.

Does this replace my issue tracker?

No. Keep the tracker you have. During bootstrap the agent asks which trackers, wikis, and specs hold your product intent, reads them through its own connectors, and cites the ticket or page behind each requirement. Kibi then connects that decision to the code that implements it, and to evidence that the code still does it.

Which languages does Kibi understand?

TypeScript and JavaScript work out of the box. Add the optional kibi-plugin-treesitter package for Python, Go, Rust, Java, C#, PHP, C, C++, Bash, Ruby, SWI-Prolog, and Terraform/HCL. It runs offline with pinned grammars, and each language is a small kibi-lang-* pack you install only if you use it. Generated files don't count toward a pack or need requirement links unless the KB uses them, and you can decline any pack. Code and source proofs read TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and SWI-Prolog directly, and through the plugin, source proofs read the imports, calls and environment reads of Go, Java, C#, Rust, PHP, C and Bash files, and the property values of PHP, C and Terraform/HCL files, without compiling them. Setup is in the plugin reference.

Can Kibi stop agents drifting from our UI design?

Partly, and only if you opt in. The experimental kibi-plugin-ui package, which /kibi-bootstrap offers when it finds React or Angular components, makes kb_check require every component to implement a design requirement, and flags a component that loses the class names or test ids that mark its agreed pattern. That catches an agent rewriting a timeline as cards. It cannot see pixels, colours or spacing; those stay with your linter. Details are in the plugin reference.

Can my agent ask Kibi what governs a change?

Yes. kb_search accepts a plain question and, alongside ranked matches, returns the current requirements that govern the topic with what each says, its recorded reason (and who gave it and when), and its linked facts, scenarios, tests, and ADRs (with an excerpt of each decision). For each requirement it also reports any contradiction or infeasible-scenario finding that names it, the approved exceptions that exempt it, and what the checks could not decide, and it names the branch and KB snapshot the answer came from. On a new branch whose store was never compiled, the answer says so and points at kibi sync instead of returning a silent empty result. Superseded and retired requirements are listed separately so they are not read as current policy, and a top match that no requirement owns is named as such rather than dressed in lower-ranked requirements. No finding is not proof: full consistency and proof status still come from kb_check, which also says how many rules it evaluated and how many fact pairs it compared, and kb_coverage. The answer is ten rows by default, and on Claude Code it is sent once, as structured content with a short text summary rather than a second JSON copy in the text.

Can my agent ask a precise question instead of searching?

Yes. kb_query asks the modeled facts directly, without the agent writing Prolog: {predicate: "permission_rule", where: {actor: "admin"}} returns each rule with its allow or deny effect, {predicate: "has_role", where: {user: "alice"}, distinct: "role"} counts a user's roles, and {subjectKey: "user.role_assignment", propertyKey: "max_roles"} returns a limit with its operator and value. {factKind: "predicate_schema"} lists the predicates and argument names the project models, an unknown argument name comes back with the declared ones, an empty answer lists the values that do exist, and every answer names the next call to make. The facts that kb_search links to a requirement carry the same typed claim and the query that asks about it, and {id, includeBody: true} returns a requirement's authored body so a stale sentence in it can be corrected.

Can my agent check a rule before writing it?

Yes. kb_upsert with dryRun: true runs the validation a real write runs, including the contradiction check for a requirement, and with plannedFacts it stages the facts kb_model planned, so an allow rule that would contradict a stored deny on the same actor, action and resource is refused before either is written, with the conflict named. kb_model also returns such a grounding as a hash-bound plan: its contradiction analysis is computed over the current knowledge base, a conflict leaves the plan blocked, and a clean plan writes the fact and its link in one kb_apply_plan call, all or nothing. kb_delete also takes dryRun: true, and deleting an authored entity first returns a hash-bound plan with the exact kb_apply_plan call that applies it.

What happens when an agent edits code a requirement owns?

With the Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ZCode, or OpenCode plugin, the pre-edit hook (OpenCode: the edit prompt) names the requirement the file implements, what it must keep true (from its linked facts), why it exists (its recorded reason, or that none is recorded), and the decision behind it (its ADR), before the change is made. With the Claude Code plugin this also covers edits the agent makes through shell commands, which get the same context right after the command runs. A superseded or retired requirement is not shown as current. After each edit the hook asks for kb_check with changed: true, which gives the verdict the pre-commit hook will give on everything changed so far, before anything is staged, and marks each finding as blocking the commit or not. kb_check scoped to the changed files also names any changed function in a file no requirement owns, so the agent records what it now does without being asked; it quotes the statement and firmness of each requirement the changed code implements, and opens with "no structural violations" rather than "no violations", because it never compares code with a requirement's prose; for a file with no linked symbols, both the hook and the check name the requirements whose titles share the file's path words, so "nothing linked" is not read as "no rule applies"; and reports conflicts it can decide, such as an allow and a deny for the same actor, action and resource, and says when an analysis is incomplete instead of calling it clean. A scenario that assumes something a current requirement forbids, on its own or only in combination with its other assumptions, is flagged and blocks proof. Conditional requirements count: "checkout may happen only when the cart total is positive" becomes a typed rule, and a checkout scenario with a zero total is flagged unless a human approved an exception for it.

Does Kibi work on a CI checkout or a detached commit?

For reading, yes. On a commit no single branch points at, such as a CI checkout of a SHA or a bisect, search, query, status, check, coverage, and graph answer from a read-only snapshot compiled from that checkout, and every answer says so. Writes are refused until you check out a branch or set KIBI_BRANCH. Details are in the CLI reference.

How do I tell what the agent wrote from what I approved?

Each entity can record its origin: written by a human, an agent, a migration or an import, and who approved it. New entities from your agent are marked as agent-written. kb_check lists agent-written requirements nobody has approved, exceptions whose approval only the agent recorded, and requirements that do not say why they exist. Kibi cannot confirm that a person approved something. It shows you what still needs your review.

Requirements and ADRs also record how firmly they were decided. A rule you stated is firm and points at your words; only another firm decision can replace it, so the agent is told to ask you first, and the agent cannot reword it in place unless it cites your new words. Kibi checks that the reference is there, not that you really wrote it. A choice you delegated, or one the agent made, is default: a later agent may replace it when it has evidence, and every replacement must say why it changed. A guess is exploratory. A rule with no firmness counts as firm unless the agent wrote it, and bootstrap marks the rules it imports from your documents as firm. When your request conflicts with any recorded rule, the agent names the rule and asks before changing it. Search results and the edit hooks show which is which.

What counts as tested, and what as proved?

A requirement is tested only when a test that claims to verify it has fresh end-to-end evidence for the current code. A passing unit test, a coverage percentage, or an old receipt does not count. The one exception is a requirement that only names a UI pattern, such as "this list is a line-and-dots timeline in both views": an isolated component test with a fresh receipt covers it, because rendering the component shows everything the requirement says. Freshness is computed from repository-relative paths and file contents, so CI and your own checkout of the same commit agree on what is tested. Tests sample cases, so tested is not proved: Kibi reserves proved for a claim a checker established for every case, with a certificate a second program can re-check. Certificate proof kinds cover enumerated domains, type-level checks, arithmetic and solver constraints, rules, state machines (including states that can never be reached and states every path must pass through), patterns, and the project's own routes, database schemas, configuration and code references, which Kibi reads itself. A requirement no current test checks is asserted when a person stands behind it and unverified when only an agent does.

Will Kibi decide the product for me?

No. kibi init creates the directory and the Git hooks; it leaves hooks it did not write alone, and with lefthook, husky or the pre-commit framework it installs none and prints the configuration to add (kibi init --print-hook all --format lefthook). It also tells agents in a fresh clone about Kibi through AGENTS.md, installs the hooks again from the package.json prepare script, and compiles a clone's store on its first query. What it commits is what you and the agent authored: symbol line positions are derived by every sync into a gitignored cache, so parallel branches do not conflict over them. It does not infer behavior. Checks prove what was encoded. Missing knowledge stays visible.

This repository publishes its own report

Every push to the default branch republishes requirement health for Kibi itself: how many current requirements are fully tested end to end, which ones rest only on someone's word, which ones contradict each other, and which evidence has gone stale.

Tested means fresh end-to-end evidence on the current code snapshot.

During bootstrap the agent asks which trackers, wikis, and specs hold your product intent, reads them through its own connectors, and cites the ticket or page behind each requirement. Kibi then connects that decision to the code that implements it, and to evidence that the code still does it. Which languages does Kibi understand? TypeScript and JavaScript work out of the box. Add the optional kibi-plugin-treesitter package for Python, Go, Rust, Java, C#, PHP, C, C++, Bash, Ruby, SWI-Prolog, and Terraform/HCL. It runs offline with pinned grammars, and each language is a small kibi-lang-* pack you install only if you use it. Generated files don't count toward a pack or need requirement links unless the KB uses them, and you can decline any pack. Code and source proofs read TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and SWI-Prolog directly, and through the plugin, source proofs read the imports, calls and environment reads of Go, Java, C#, Rust, PHP, C and Bash files, and the property values of PHP, C and Terraform/HCL files, without compiling them. Setup is in the plugin reference. Can Kibi stop agents drifting from our UI design? Partly, and only if you opt in. The experimental kibi-plugin-ui package, which /kibi-bootstrap offers when it finds React or Angular components, makes kb_check require every component to implement a design requirement, and flags a component that loses the class names or test ids that mark its agreed pattern. That catches an agent rewriting a timeline as cards. It cannot see pixels, colours or spacing; those stay with your linter. Details are in the plugin reference. Can my agent ask Kibi what governs a change? Yes. kb_search accepts a plain question and, alongside ranked matches, returns the current requirements that govern the topic with what each says, its recorded reason (and who gave it and when), and its linked facts, scenarios, tests, and ADRs (with an excerpt of each decision). For each requirement it also reports any contradiction or infeasible-scenario finding that names it, the approved exceptions that exempt it, and what the checks could not decide, and it names the branch and KB snapshot the answer came from. On a new branch whose store was never compiled, the answer says so and points at kibi sync instead of returning a silent empty result. Superseded and retired requirements are listed separately so they are not read as current policy, and a top match that no requirement owns is named as such rather than dressed in lower-ranked requirements. No finding is not proof: full consistency and proof status still come from kb_check, which also says how many rules it evaluated and how many fact pairs it compared, and kb_coverage. The answer is ten rows by default, and on Claude Code it is sent once, as structured content with a short text summary rather than a second JSON copy in the text. Can my agent ask a precise question instead of searching? Yes. kb_query asks the modeled facts directly, without the agent writing Prolog: {predicate: "permission_rule", where: {actor: "admin"}} returns each rule with its allow or deny effect, {predicate: "has_role", where: {user: "alice"}, distinct: "role"} counts a user's roles, and {subjectKey: "user.role_assignment", propertyKey: "max_roles"} returns a limit with its operator and value. {factKind: "predicate_schema"} lists the predicates and argument names the project models, an unknown argument name comes back with the declared ones, an empty answer lists the values that do exist, and every answer names the next call to make. The facts that kb_search links to a requirement carry the same typed claim and the query that asks about it, and {id, includeBody: true} returns a requirement's authored body so a stale sentence in it can be corrected. Can my agent check a rule before writing it? Yes. kb_upsert with dryRun: true runs the validation a real write runs, including the contradiction check for a requirement, and with plannedFacts it stages the facts kb_model planned, so an allow rule that would contradict a stored deny on the same actor, action and resource is refused before either is written, with the conflict named. kb_model also returns such a grounding as a hash-bound plan: its contradiction analysis is computed over the current knowledge base, a conflict leaves the plan blocked, and a clean plan writes the fact and its link in one kb_apply_plan call, all or nothing. kb_delete also takes dryRun: true, and deleting an authored entity first returns a hash-bound plan with the exact kb_apply_plan call that applies it. What happens when an agent edits code a requirement owns? With the Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ZCode, or OpenCode plugin, the pre-edit hook (OpenCode: the edit prompt) names the requirement the file implements, what it must keep true (from its linked facts), why it exists (its recorded reason, or that none is recorded), and the decision behind it (its ADR), before the change is made. With the Claude Code plugin this also covers edits the agent makes through shell commands, which get the same context right after the command runs. A superseded or retired requirement is not shown as current. After each edit the hook asks for kb_check with changed: true, which gives the verdict the pre-commit hook will give on everything changed so far, before anything is staged, and marks each finding as blocking the commit or not. kb_check scoped to the changed files also names any changed function in a file no requirement owns, so the agent records what it now does without being asked; it quotes the statement and firmness of each requirement the changed code implements, and opens with "no structural violations" rather than "no violations", because it never compares code with a requirement's prose; for a file with no linked symbols, both the hook and the check name the requirements whose titles share the file's path words, so "nothing linked" is not read as "no rule applies"; and reports conflicts it can decide, such as an allow and a deny for the same actor, action and resource, and says when an analysis is incomplete instead of calling it clean. A scenario that assumes something a current requirement forbids, on its own or only in combination with its other assumptions, is flagged and blocks proof. Conditional requirements count: "checkout may happen only when the cart total is positive" becomes a typed rule, and a checkout scenario with a zero total is flagged unless a human approved an exception for it. Does Kibi work on a CI checkout or a detached commit? For reading, yes. On a commit no single branch points at, such as a CI checkout of a SHA or a bisect, search, query, status, check, coverage, and graph answer from a read-only snapshot compiled from that checkout, and every answer says so. Writes are refused until you check out a branch or set KIBI_BRANCH. Details are in the CLI reference. How do I tell what the agent wrote from what I approved? Each entity can record its origin: written by a human, an agent, a migration or an import, and who approved it. New entities from your agent are marked as agent-written. kb_check lists agent-written requirements nobody has approved, exceptions whose approval only the agent recorded, and requirements that do not say why they exist. Kibi cannot confirm that a person approved something. It shows you what still needs your review. Requirements and ADRs also record how firmly they were decided. A rule you stated is firm and points at your words; only another firm decision can replace it, so the agent is told to ask you first, and the agent cannot reword it in place unless it cites your new words. Kibi checks that the reference is there, not that you really wrote it. A choice you delegated, or one the agent made, is default: a later agent may replace it when it has evidence, and every replacement must say why it changed. A guess is exploratory. A rule with no firmness counts as firm unless the agent wrote it, and bootstrap marks the rules it imports from your documents as firm. When your request conflicts with any recorded rule, the agent names the rule and asks before changing it. Search results and the edit hooks show which is which. What counts as tested, and what as proved? A requirement is tested only when a test that claims to verify it has fresh end-to-end evidence for the current code. A passing unit test, a coverage percentage, or an old receipt does not count. The one exception is a requirement that only names a UI pattern, such as "this list is a line-and-dots timeline in both views": an isolated component test with a fresh receipt covers it, because rendering the component shows everything the requirement says. Freshness is computed from repository-relative paths and file contents, so CI and your own checkout of the same commit agree on what is tested. Tests sample cases, so tested is not proved: Kibi reserves proved for a claim a checker established for every case, with a certificate a second program can re-check. Certificate proof kinds cover enumerated domains, type-level checks, arithmetic and solver constraints, rules, state machines (including states that can never be reached and states every path must pass through), patterns, and the project's own routes, database schemas, configuration and code references, which Kibi reads itself. A requirement no current test checks is asserted when a person stands behind it and unverified when only an agent does. Will Kibi decide the product for me? No. kibi init creates the directory and the Git hooks; it leaves hooks it did not write alone, and with lefthook, husky or the pre-commit framework it installs none and prints the configuration to add (kibi init --print-hook all --format lefthook). It also tells agents in a fresh clone about Kibi through AGENTS.md, installs the hooks again from the package.json prepare script, and compiles a clone's store on its first query. What it commits is what you and the agent authored: symbol line positions are derived by every sync into a gitignored cache, so parallel branches do not conflict over them. It does not infer behavior. Checks prove what was encoded. Missing knowledge stays visible. This repository publishes its own report Every push to the default branch republishes requirement health for Kibi itself: how many current requirements are fully tested end to end, which ones rest only on someone's word, which ones contradict each other, and which evidence has gone stale. Tested means fresh end-to-end evidence on the current code snapshot. Open the live report Start with one prompt. Paste the setup prompt into your agent, approve the plan it shows you, and read your first health report. Prompt the intent. Kibi makes the agent remember it—and prove the implementation.

blocks.html_en: A requirement is tested only when a test that claims to verify it has fresh end-to-end evidence for the current code. A passing unit test, a coverage percentage, or an old receipt does not count. The one exception is a requirement that only names a UI pattern, such as "this list is a line-and-dots timeline in both views": an isolated component test with a fresh receipt covers it, because rendering the component shows everything the requirement says. Freshness is computed from repository-relative paths and file contents, so CI and your own checkout of the same commit agree on what is tested. Tests sample cases, so tested is not proved: Kibi reserves proved for a claim a checker established for every case, with a certificate a second program can re-check. Certificate proof kinds cover enumerated domains, type-level checks, arithmetic and solver constraints, rules, state machines (including states that can never be reached and states every path must pass through), patterns, and the project's own routes, database schemas, configuration and code references, which Kibi reads itself. A requirement no current test checks is asserted when a person stands behind it and unverified when only an agent does.

content_html_zh:
Open source · runs in your repository

Say what the software should do. Your agent won’t forget why.

Kibi is a requirements framework for AI coding agents. It records the reasoning behind your code (the intent, assumptions and trade-offs you agreed in the chat) as requirements in your repository, links them to the code and tests, and makes every later agent respect them.

  • Keeps the why behind each change, not just the what
  • Shows the agent that reasoning before it edits the code
  • Refuses new rules that contradict old ones
  • Reports which requirements are actually tested

Each line is a requirement riding to the gate. Only fresh end-to-end evidence clears it.

01The problem

Code shows what the software does. Not what it must keep doing.

In source, every line looks equally deliberate. A hard-won trade-off, a business rule, a temporary assumption, a shortcut and a forgotten leftover all read the same. The difference lived in the conversation where they were decided, and that conversation is gone. So the next agent either “cleans up” a decision or carefully preserves an accident.

With KibiEach requirement records why it exists, in the words of whoever asked, and decisions keep their trade-offs. When you state a rule, the agent records it in one kb_record call with your reason, your words and the code that implements it, and learns at once whether a commit would pass. They live in .kb/ beside the code on every branch, and Kibi flags requirements that do not say why.
  • 02 Decisions stop getting undone WithoutThe agent rewrites a rule it never knew existed. With KibiBefore it edits a file, the agent is shown the requirement that code implements, what it must keep true, why it exists, and the decision behind it.
  • 03 Conflicts are caught before the code WithoutTwo prompts a week apart contradict each other, and nobody notices. With KibiA rule that contradicts an existing one is refused with both named, and you decide which wins.
  • 04 “Done” means tested, not claimed WithoutGreen CI does not say which product behavior still works on this commit. With KibiThe health report shows which requirements have fresh end-to-end evidence, which rest only on someone’s word, and which have gaps.

02Why not a memory file

Memory remembers. Kibi enforces.

Notes files and memory servers help an agent recall things. Kibi turns intent and its reasons into rules that are linked to code, checked for contradictions, put in front of the agent at edit time, and backed by evidence.

03How it works

From prompt to proof, on one rail

Kibi keeps intent attached to the work at every stage, and it is conservative about the last one.

  1. IntentYou say it oncePrompt the behavior in plain words, the way you already do. That sentence stays the source.
  2. RequirementsThe agent writes it downRequirements, scenarios and typed facts land in .kb/ beside the code, citing the ticket or page they came from.
  3. EnforcementEvery edit hears itHooks name the requirement before an agent edits the code that implements it. Checks flag contradictions and untraced code.
  4. EvidenceTests leave receiptsA test that claims a requirement records evidence tied to the exact code snapshot it ran on.
  5. ProofOnly fresh evidence passesStale receipts and passing unit tests do not clear the gate. Proved is reserved for claims a checker established for every case.

04Your part

What you actually do

Three things, and none of them is filling in a requirements form.

  1. 01State the behavior Prompt the way you already do. “Draft edits must save when someone navigates away.” You do not fill in a requirements form.
  2. 02Approve real decisions The agent proposes a plan before it writes project knowledge. You approve it, or you correct the product call. A plan compiled from your prompt lands in full or not at all, and the bookkeeping stays with the agent.
  3. 03Read the result The health report names what is tested, what still has a gap, and what contradicts itself, and labels each requirement proved, tested, asserted or unverified. A green test run is a different fact. When the pre-commit hook refuses new code no requirement owns, it prints one block per declaration with the requirements that already own the rest of its file and a ready-to-run input that links it, never a pick of its own.

05Setup

Add Kibi to the repository

Kibi is driven by your coding agent, so the recommended setup is a prompt. Your agent installs the packages, runs kibi init, connects itself to Kibi, and bootstraps the knowledge base behind a plan you approve, then adds scenarios, predicates and the claims the plan could not write in the normal workflow, and proposes how proof runs for your test runner in a second plan you approve. The package-manager tabs are the manual route; re-running kibi init completes missing directories and schema files while preserving existing knowledge and schema files. It does not invent what the product does.

The agent first asks where your product intent lives, such as issue trackers, wikis and specs, and which sources to trust. Every requirement in the bootstrap plan cites the ticket or page it came from, and nothing is written until you approve the plan. When a claim sits next to an existing requirement on the same topic that Kibi cannot check logically, the plan names that requirement so the agent compares the two, including for claims the plan leaves for the agent to write. How plans are built, applied and resumed after an interruption is in the MCP reference.

The bootstrap records the code that decides each behavior, not every declaration. The pre-commit hook judges a commit only on the declarations it adds or changes, so an agent's correct change is never refused over gaps it did not create; kibi check counts the unrecorded rest as non-blocking symbol debt (kibi check --symbol-debt lists it), and it shrinks as commits touch that code.

Requires Node.js 22+. SWI-Prolog is bundled on Linux (x64, arm64) and macOS; other platforms need swipl (SWI-Prolog 9.0+) on your PATH. A system swipl is only a fallback; set KIBI_SWIPL=system to prefer it. Bun commands and per-platform setup are in the installation guide. Each release has one version, such as Kibi 2026.11.0, that names its exact package set; kibi --version and kibi doctor show it (release versions), and the CLI tells you once a day when a newer one is out (update notices). Kibi sends anonymous usage statistics; see what is sent and how to turn it off.

07FAQ

Questions people ask first

The short answers. The guide has the long ones.

Do I write the requirements myself?

No. You describe the behavior. Your agent turns that into requirements, scenarios, tests, and links to the code. You step in when the product decision is actually ambiguous.

Does this replace my issue tracker?

No. Keep the tracker you have. During bootstrap the agent asks which trackers, wikis, and specs hold your product intent, reads them through its own connectors, and cites the ticket or page behind each requirement. Kibi then connects that decision to the code that implements it, and to evidence that the code still does it.

Which languages does Kibi understand?

TypeScript and JavaScript work out of the box. Add the optional kibi-plugin-treesitter package for Python, Go, Rust, Java, C#, PHP, C, C++, Bash, Ruby, SWI-Prolog, and Terraform/HCL. It runs offline with pinned grammars, and each language is a small kibi-lang-* pack you install only if you use it. Generated files don't count toward a pack or need requirement links unless the KB uses them, and you can decline any pack. Code and source proofs read TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and SWI-Prolog directly, and through the plugin, source proofs read the imports, calls and environment reads of Go, Java, C#, Rust, PHP, C and Bash files, and the property values of PHP, C and Terraform/HCL files, without compiling them. Setup is in the plugin reference.

Can Kibi stop agents drifting from our UI design?

Partly, and only if you opt in. The experimental kibi-plugin-ui package, which /kibi-bootstrap offers when it finds React or Angular components, makes kb_check require every component to implement a design requirement, and flags a component that loses the class names or test ids that mark its agreed pattern. That catches an agent rewriting a timeline as cards. It cannot see pixels, colours or spacing; those stay with your linter. Details are in the plugin reference.

Can my agent ask Kibi what governs a change?

是的。 kb_search accepts a plain question and, alongside ranked matches, returns the current requirements that govern the topic with what each says, its recorded reason (and who gave it and when), and its linked facts, scenarios, tests, and ADRs (with an excerpt of each decision). For each requirement it also reports any contradiction or infeasible-scenario finding that names it, the approved exceptions that exempt it, and what the checks could not decide, and it names the branch and KB snapshot the answer came from. On a new branch whose store was never compiled, the answer says so and points at kibi sync instead of returning a silent empty result. Superseded and retired requirements are listed separately so they are not read as current policy, and a top match that no requirement owns is named as such rather than dressed in lower-ranked requirements. No finding is not proof: full consistency and proof status still come from kb_check, which also says how many rules it evaluated and how many fact pairs it compared, and kb_coverage. The answer is ten rows by default, and on Claude Code it is sent once, as structured content with a short text summary rather than a second JSON copy in the text.

Can my agent ask a precise question instead of searching?

是的。 kb_query asks the modeled facts directly, without the agent writing Prolog: {predicate: "permission_rule", where: {actor: "admin"}} returns each rule with its allow or deny effect, {predicate: "has_role", where: {user: "alice"}, distinct: "role"} counts a user's roles, and {subjectKey: "user.role_assignment", propertyKey: "max_roles"} returns a limit with its operator and value. {factKind: "predicate_schema"} lists the predicates and argument names the project models, an unknown argument name comes back with the declared ones, an empty answer lists the values that do exist, and every answer names the next call to make. The facts that kb_search links to a requirement carry the same typed claim and the query that asks about it, and {id, includeBody: true} returns a requirement's authored body so a stale sentence in it can be corrected.

Can my agent check a rule before writing it?

是的。 kb_upsert with dryRun: true runs the validation a real write runs, including the contradiction check for a requirement, and with plannedFacts it stages the facts kb_model planned, so an allow rule that would contradict a stored deny on the same actor, action and resource is refused before either is written, with the conflict named. kb_model also returns such a grounding as a hash-bound plan: its contradiction analysis is computed over the current knowledge base, a conflict leaves the plan blocked, and a clean plan writes the fact and its link in one kb_apply_plan call, all or nothing. kb_delete also takes dryRun: true, and deleting an authored entity first returns a hash-bound plan with the exact kb_apply_plan call that applies it.

What happens when an agent edits code a requirement owns?

With the Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ZCode, or OpenCode plugin, the pre-edit hook (OpenCode: the edit prompt) names the requirement the file implements, what it must keep true (from its linked facts), why it exists (its recorded reason, or that none is recorded), and the decision behind it (its ADR), before the change is made. With the Claude Code plugin this also covers edits the agent makes through shell commands, which get the same context right after the command runs. A superseded or retired requirement is not shown as current. After each edit the hook asks for kb_check with changed: true, which gives the verdict the pre-commit hook will give on everything changed so far, before anything is staged, and marks each finding as blocking the commit or not. kb_check scoped to the changed files also names any changed function in a file no requirement owns, so the agent records what it now does without being asked; it quotes the statement and firmness of each requirement the changed code implements, and opens with "no structural violations" rather than "no violations", because it never compares code with a requirement's prose; for a file with no linked symbols, both the hook and the check name the requirements whose titles share the file's path words, so "nothing linked" is not read as "no rule applies"; and reports conflicts it can decide, such as an allow and a deny for the same actor, action and resource, and says when an analysis is incomplete instead of calling it clean. A scenario that assumes something a current requirement forbids, on its own or only in combination with its other assumptions, is flagged and blocks proof. Conditional requirements count: "checkout may happen only when the cart total is positive" becomes a typed rule, and a checkout scenario with a zero total is flagged unless a human approved an exception for it.

Does Kibi work on a CI checkout or a detached commit?

For reading, yes. On a commit no single branch points at, such as a CI checkout of a SHA or a bisect, search, query, status, check, coverage, and graph answer from a read-only snapshot compiled from that checkout, and every answer says so. Writes are refused until you check out a branch or set KIBI_BRANCH. Details are in the CLI reference.

How do I tell what the agent wrote from what I approved?

Each entity can record its origin: written by a human, an agent, a migration or an import, and who approved it. New entities from your agent are marked as agent-written. kb_check lists agent-written requirements nobody has approved, exceptions whose approval only the agent recorded, and requirements that do not say why they exist. Kibi cannot confirm that a person approved something. It shows you what still needs your review.

Requirements and ADRs also record how firmly they were decided. A rule you stated is firm and points at your words; only another firm decision can replace it, so the agent is told to ask you first, and the agent cannot reword it in place unless it cites your new words. Kibi checks that the reference is there, not that you really wrote it. A choice you delegated, or one the agent made, is default: a later agent may replace it when it has evidence, and every replacement must say why it changed. A guess is exploratory. A rule with no firmness counts as firm unless the agent wrote it, and bootstrap marks the rules it imports from your documents as firm. When your request conflicts with any recorded rule, the agent names the rule and asks before changing it. Search results and the edit hooks show which is which.

What counts as tested, and what as proved?

A requirement is tested only when a test that claims to verify it has fresh end-to-end evidence for the current code. A passing unit test, a coverage percentage, or an old receipt does not count. The one exception is a requirement that only names a UI pattern, such as "this list is a line-and-dots timeline in both views": an isolated component test with a fresh receipt covers it, because rendering the component shows everything the requirement says. Freshness is computed from repository-relative paths and file contents, so CI and your own checkout of the same commit agree on what is tested. Tests sample cases, so tested is not proved: Kibi reserves proved for a claim a checker established for every case, with a certificate a second program can re-check. Certificate proof kinds cover enumerated domains, type-level checks, arithmetic and solver constraints, rules, state machines (including states that can never be reached and states every path must pass through), patterns, and the project's own routes, database schemas, configuration and code references, which Kibi reads itself. A requirement no current test checks is asserted when a person stands behind it and unverified when only an agent does.

Will Kibi decide the product for me?

No. kibi init creates the directory and the Git hooks; it leaves hooks it did not write alone, and with lefthook, husky or the pre-commit framework it installs none and prints the configuration to add (kibi init --print-hook all --format lefthook). It also tells agents in a fresh clone about Kibi through AGENTS.md, installs the hooks again from the package.json prepare script, and compiles a clone's store on its first query. What it commits is what you and the agent authored: symbol line positions are derived by every sync into a gitignored cache, so parallel branches do not conflict over them. It does not infer behavior. Checks prove what was encoded. Missing knowledge stays visible.
